pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11y; fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers up to 4-digit × 2-digit using formal long multiplication, explaining each partial product.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'multiply multi-digit numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit whole number using the formal written method of long multiplication'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.5 — 'fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm'.
• Operational details — by Y6 the area-model scaffolding is largely internalised; the goal is FLUENT, accurate execution of 4-digit × 2-digit (2463×37) and the ability to EXPLAIN each partial product and the placeholder shift. The two partial-product rows are ×ones and ×tens; errors are now overwhelmingly procedural — lost placeholder zero, carry mistakes across many columns, misaligned addition. Fluency practice should pair speed/accuracy with a retained conceptual check (relate to the area model / estimate) so slips are caught. Estimate first (2463×37 ≈ 2500×40 = 100000).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 3-digit × 2-digit accurately with correct placeholder. Tier B (age 10–11): 4-digit × 2-digit (2463×37) fluently and checked against an estimate. Tier C (age 11): explain each partial product's place value and diagnose a planted error in a worked long multiplication.
bestPractices: Prioritise fluent, accurate execution while retaining the area-model rationale for the two rows and the placeholder zero, so errors remain self-diagnosable.
Estimate first (round both factors) and check the final answer against it to catch place-value slips.
Target the common procedural errors explicitly — missing placeholder zero, multi-column carries, misaligned partial-product addition — through error-spotting practice.
Require explanation of each partial product's place value, not just a correct answer, to keep procedure and meaning linked.
Check via the inverse or estimation and build accuracy under increasing digit-length.
keyRepresentations: Compact long-multiplication layout with the placeholder zero
Area/grid model (as an internalised check, revisited on error)
Estimation (rounding both factors) to bound the product
Partial-product annotation (×ones row, ×tens row) for explanation
commonMisconceptions: Omitting the placeholder zero on the ×tens partial product.
Carry errors accumulating across many columns in large calculations.
Misaligning the partial products when adding them.
Multiplying by only one digit of the two-digit multiplier.
Executing fluently but with no conceptual check, so a wrong-magnitude answer slips through.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year-olds: fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers (up to 4-digit × 2-digit, e.g. 2463×37) using formal long multiplication, explaining each partial product and the placeholder zero. By this stage the area-model scaffold is largely internalised; the aim is accurate, confident execution paired with a retained conceptual check (estimate and area model) so place-value slips are caught. Target the common procedural errors directly — missing placeholder zero, multi-column carry mistakes, misaligned addition, or multiplying by only one digit of the two-digit factor — and require learners to say what each row represents.

activities.title: Step-by-step long multiplication with an estimate check
feedback: If the ×tens row comes out about ten times too small, you probably dropped the placeholder zero — remember that row is 2463 groups of thirty, so it must start in the tens column; the zero holds the ones place.

If one digit of a partial product is wrong, slow down the carries: write each carry above the correct column and re-check it. Your estimate (~100000) only catches errors that change the size of the final answer; a single wrong digit can still give a plausible-looking total, so re-check each multiplication and carry directly.
If you multiplied by only one digit of 37, remember 37 = 30 + 7, so you need one row for ×7 and one for ×30.
If the answer is correct but you cannot say what each row means, link back to the area model: 2463 splits into (2463×30) and (2463×7), and the two parts recombine when you add.
activities.rationale: Y6/Grade 5 standards require fluent, accurate use of the standard algorithm; pairing step-by-step execution with an estimate and area-model check keeps procedure and meaning linked so procedural slips remain self-diagnosable.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils multiply multi-digit numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal long multiplication.
5.NBT.5 requires fluently multiplying multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.
Fluency should retain a conceptual check (area model/estimation) so procedural errors like the missing placeholder zero remain self-diagnosable.
learnerActions: Before calculating, estimate 2463×37 by rounding both factors: 2500×40 = 100000, and write this down as the expected ballpark.
Work 2463×37 by long multiplication, writing the ×ones row (2463×7 = 17241) and the ×tens row underneath.
When starting the ×tens row, write the placeholder zero in the ones column first, then multiply by 3 tens to get 73890.
Add the two rows: 17241 + 73890 = 91131, keeping the columns aligned.
Compare the final answer with your estimate of ~100000 — 91131 is in the right ballpark, so the magnitude is plausible.
At each step, check that any carry is jotted above the correct column and added into the next multiplication.
activities.intendedInsight: Each partial-product row multiplies the whole of 2463 by a part of 37 (by 7 ones, then by 30), and the rows are added to recombine the parts. The placeholder zero is there because the second row is really ×30, not ×3. The estimate bounds the answer's size, so a lost zero shows up as a clearly wrong magnitude. A carry slip usually changes only one or two digits and can still look plausible, so it has to be caught by checking the working itself.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and fill-the-gap in a worked long multiplication
feedback: Missing placeholder zero: the ×tens row is ten times too small; it must begin in the tens column.
Misaligned addition: re-align each row by place value (ones under ones, tens under tens) before summing.
Carry error: check each carried digit is above and added into the correct next column.
For a fill-in-the-blank partial product, compute it directly and confirm it is consistent with the neighbouring digits and the carries recorded.

For the estimate, round each factor to one significant figure and multiply: 5000×30 = 150000. The exact product 4762×28 = 133336 sits below this estimate — because rounding both factors up gives an over-estimate, the true answer should fall under it.
activities.rationale: Error-spotting, gap-filling, and estimate selection consolidate and assess the specific procedural slips that dominate at this stage. This is assessment/consolidation of fixed examples rather than feedback on a learner's own live working.
sourceClaims: Fluency should retain a conceptual check (area model/estimation) so procedural errors like the missing placeholder zero remain self-diagnosable.
learnerActions: Examine worked examples of 4-digit × 2-digit long multiplication that contain a single planted mistake.
Identify the error type: a missing placeholder zero, a misaligned partial-product addition, a dropped or misplaced carry, or multiplying by only one digit.
Complete a fill-in-the-blank worked example where one partial product (or one digit of a partial product) is left empty, computing the missing value and checking it against the rest of the working.
Estimate the correct answer by rounding both factors, and use it to judge whether the worked total is plausible before pinpointing the error.
Rewrite the step correctly and recompute the final total.
Choose the best estimate for a calculation such as 4762×28 from a short list of magnitudes, justifying the rounding used (≈5000×30 = 150000).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to diagnose a planted error or complete a missing step shows you understand each step's role — especially why the ×tens row is shifted by a placeholder zero and why rows must be aligned before adding. Estimation is a fast first filter for implausible answers.

activities.title: Annotate each partial product with its place value
feedback: If the explanation of the zero is 'that's just the rule', push further: the second row multiplies by 3 tens, so its smallest place is tens — the zero holds the empty ones place.
If the rows are not matched to area regions, draw the split 37 = 30 + 7 and show each part covering the full width 2463.
activities.rationale: A static annotated worked example is a strong reference for the explanation demand, keeping the compact algorithm linked to the area-model conceptual check; it cannot, however, give feedback on the learner's own fluent execution, so use it alongside live practice.
sourceClaims: Fluency should retain a conceptual check (area model/estimation) so procedural errors like the missing placeholder zero remain self-diagnosable.
learnerActions: Take a completed long multiplication of 2463×37 and label the first row '×7 (ones)' and the second row '×30 (tens)'.
Explain in writing or aloud why there is a zero at the end of the second row.
Match each partial-product row to the corresponding region of an area/grid model: the rectangle 2463×30 and the rectangle 2463×7.
State why the two rows are added together to get the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Each row corresponds to multiplying the whole number by a part of the multiplier; the placeholder zero marks that the second part is tens. Connecting the compact algorithm to the area model keeps the procedure meaningful.

constraints: Learners must actually perform the multiplication and explain each row; recognition-only or multiple-choice formats can assess or consolidate classification of errors but do not themselves elicit independent construction of the algorithm.

Annotated worked examples, gap-fill, and spot-the-error tasks use fixed examples: they build reference understanding and diagnosis but do not give feedback on a learner's own live working — pair them with learner-generated calculations.
Estimation bounds magnitude but does not confirm exact correctness; use it as a first filter, then verify the full computation.

Tier the digit length: 3-digit × 2-digit with correct placeholder first, then 4-digit × 2-digit fluently and checked against an estimate, then explain each partial product's place value and diagnose a planted error.
Any 'show why' area-model link should be available on demand when a step goes wrong, not forced on every step, so fluent learners are not slowed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Independent re-audit of arithmetic: 2463×7 = 17241; 2463×30 = 73890; 17241 + 73890 = 91131, matching the assessment's stated values. 4762×28 = 133336. No arithmetic errors found.

Estimate check: 2500×40 = 100000 (both factors rounded up) and 91131 sits plausibly below it; 5000×30 = 150000 is likewise an upper over-estimate for 4762×28 (actual 133336, about 11% under). Feedback wording was corrected to state the actual value and the direction of the bound.
Source status unchanged: CCSS 5.NBT.5 and the NCETM guidance were marked unverified in the original and are retained only as curriculum-requirement / conceptual-check attributions, not upgraded.

The original material asserted '3D adds no value' and that dialogue 'can't' support a multi-digit algorithm; these catalog-fit judgements are not treated as universal pedagogical laws and have been omitted rather than restated as facts.

probeDeeper: What does the second row of your working (73,890) represent?
Why do you add the two rows together at the end?
Estimate 2,463 × 37 roughly — is 91,131 in the right ballpark?
Where did the placeholder zero come from, and what would happen without it?
assess.correctAnswer: 2,463 × 37 = 91,131 (2463×7 = 17,241; 2463×30 = 73,890; sum 91,131). The teacher watches for a fluent, error-free execution: correct partial products, the placeholder zero on the ×30 row, accurate carrying across four digits, and correct addition — plus the child explaining the first row is ×7 and the second is ×30.

errorPatterns.pattern: omits or misplaces the placeholder zero on the tens-digit row
errorPatterns.nextMove: reinforce that the second row multiplies by 3 TENS, so it must start in the tens column — write the zero to hold the ones place; connect to 'thirty groups'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: second partial product ten times too small; total wildly off

errorPatterns.pattern: carrying errors compound across the four digits — a carry dropped or added into the wrong column
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach the method; slow the carries, jotting each above the correct column, and check against the estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one digit of a partial product wrong; estimate (2500×40 = 100,000) flags it

errorPatterns.pattern: executes correctly but cannot explain what each row represents or why they are summed — pure rote
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach steps; link to the area model — the number splits into 30 and 7, each multiplies the whole 2463, and the parts recombine.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right answer, but 'why add the two rows?' draws a blank

responseLevels.gap: makes placeholder/carrying errors that derail the calculation; cannot explain the partial products.
responseLevels.full: computes 4-digit × 2-digit fluently and accurately, explains each partial product and the summation, and checks against an estimate.
responseLevels.partial: reaches the correct answer but only slowly or with a self-corrected slip, or executes fluently yet cannot say what the rows mean.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 2,463 × 37 by long multiplication while you watch, then to point at each partial product row and tell you what it represents and why the two rows are added. Watch fluency, the placeholder zero, carrying across four digits, and the final column addition.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: At this stage the objective is FLUENCY without procedural errors plus understanding what each partial product means. Watching a four-by-two-digit case surfaces both accuracy (placeholder, carries) and comprehension (can the child say the second row is 2463 groups of thirty?) — a rote executor computes but cannot explain the rows.
